papers.title: Improving LLM Outputs Against Jailbreak Attacks With Expert Model Integration
papers.abstract: Using LLMs in a production environment presents security challenges that include vulnerabilities to jailbreaks and prompt injections, which can result in harmful outputs for humans or the enterprise. The challenge is amplified when working within a specific domain, as topics generally accepted for LLMs to address, may be irrelevant to that field. These problems can be mitigated for example, by fine-tuning large language models with domain-specific and security-focused data. However, these alone are insufficient, as jailbreak techniques evolve. Additionally, API-accessed models do not offer the flexibility needed to tailor behavior to industry-specific objectives, and in-context learning is not always sufficient and reliable. In response to these challenges, we introduce Archias, an expert model, adept at distinguishing between in-domain and out-of-domain communications. Archias classifies user inquiries into several categories: in-domain (specifically for the automotive industry), malicious questions, price injections, prompt injections, and out-of-domain examples. Our methodology integrates outputs from the expert model (Archias) into prompts, which are then processed by the LLM to generate responses. This method increases the model’s ability to understand the user’s intention and give appropriate answers. Archias can be adjusted, fine-tuned, and used for many different purposes due to its small size. Therefore, it can be simply customized to the needs of any industry. To validate our approach, we created a benchmark dataset for the automotive industry. Furthermore, in the interest of advancing research and development, we release our benchmark dataset to the community.

papers.summary: The researchers introduce Archias, a BERT-based expert that classifies requests into automotive-domain and security-related categories. Its predictions are incorporated into prompts sent to a downstream language model, helping that model interpret user intent. A manually crafted 150-example multiple-choice benchmark supports their evaluation, and the authors report improved output quality from expert integration. They acknowledge that open-ended interactions, larger benchmarks and edge cases need further study. For HMEG, this is evidence for investigating specialized pre-generation signals, not a reproduction of the same pipeline. HMEG’s five classifiers produce a guardrail decision through routing and fusion rather than directly modifying a target LLM’s prompt.

papers.methodology: A fine-tuned BERT expert classifies requests into domain and security categories; its outputs are inserted into downstream LLM prompts.

papers.results: The authors report improved response quality with expert-output ingestion. The 88% benchmark score described on p. 5 is human performance, not detector accuracy.
papers.limitations: The authors call for larger test sets, open-ended evaluation and broader real-world testing; edge-case misclassification remains.

papers.title: Benchmarking and Defending Against Indirect Prompt Injection Attacks on Large Language Models
papers.venue: Proceedings of the 31st ACM SIGKDD Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining (KDD 2025)
papers.abstractPermission: Original abstract linked at the official source; republication permission has not been verified.
papers.summary: BIPIA studies attacks hidden in external material that an LLM application reads while completing a legitimate task. The benchmark covers five application scenarios and 250 attacker goals, and the authors evaluate 25 language models. They identify confusion between data and instructions as a central weakness. Their defenses encourage boundary awareness and explicitly remind the model not to follow instructions embedded in untrusted content, with approaches for both black-box and white-box settings. The paper reports vulnerability across evaluated models and improvements from the defenses. For HMEG, this motivates source-aware instruction-manipulation tests; it does not establish that classifying isolated prompts provides complete application-level protection.

papers.methodology: Build BIPIA application scenarios; evaluate protected tasks under injected external content; test boundary-awareness and explicit-reminder defenses.
models: 25 evaluated LLMs, including GPT-3.5-turbo and GPT-4
datasets: BIPIA: five application scenarios and 250 attacker goals
papers.results: The paper reports varying susceptibility across the 25 evaluated LLMs and reduced attack success with boundary-awareness and explicit-reminder defenses. This is application-level indirect-injection evaluation, not binary prompt accuracy.
papers.limitations: Not specified in the source.
papers.opportunity: Evaluate HMEG instruction-manipulation signals with explicit trusted/untrusted context and report the limits of isolated-prompt classification.
papers.findings: Separating informational context from actionable instructions is central to indirect-injection defense.

papers.title: Building Guardrails for Large Language Models
papers.source: Building Guardrails for Large Language Models - 2402.01822v2.pdf
papers.abstractPermission: Abstract not republished; follow the official source link.
papers.summary: This position paper asks how guardrails should be engineered for real applications rather than judged only by a single benchmark score. It reviews Llama Guard, NeMo and Guardrails AI and discusses risks involving harmful outputs, fairness, privacy and uncertainty. It proposes a systematic process that begins with requirements, considers learning and symbolic mechanisms, and connects development to verification and testing. It is not a new prompt classifier trained on a reported benchmark corpus. For HMEG, the useful lesson is methodological: define the English-language scope, document assumptions, and evaluate false positives and computation alongside security. The paper does not validate HMEG’s particular architecture.

papers.title: Comparative evaluation of machine learning methods for protecting LLMs from prompt injection attacks
papers.abstractPermission: Original abstract linked at the official source; republication permission has not been verified.
papers.summary: The authors compare several ways to detect prompt injection: traditional classifiers using embeddings, independently fine-tuned transformers, existing specialized detectors and general language models. They select the jayavibhav/prompt-injection corpus, containing 327,400 queries, after reviewing four candidate datasets. Fine-tuned transformers provide strong balanced performance in this benchmark, while the traditional models differ considerably. For example, the reported LightGBM accuracy is 90.42% and random-forest accuracy is 83.07%. The authors warn that reliance on one balanced dataset limits real-world generalization. For HMEG, the paper supports using several standalone baselines and testing cross-source transfer. Its results are literature evidence, not measurements of HMEG.

papers.title: The Dangerous Effects of a Frustratingly Easy LLMs Jailbreak Attack
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are employed in various applications, including direct end-user interactions. Ideally, they should consistently generate both factually accurate and non-offensive responses, and they are specifically trained and safeguarded to meet these standards. However, this paper demonstrates that simple, manual, and generalizable jailbreaking attacks, such as reasoning backward, can effectively bypass the safeguards implemented in LLMs, potentially leading to harmful consequences. These include the dissemination of misinformation, the amplification of harmful recommendations, and toxic comments. Furthermore, these attacks have been found to reveal latent biases within LLMs, raising concerns about their ethical and societal implications. In particular, the vulnerabilities exposed by such attacks appear to be generalizable across different LLMs and languages. This paper also assesses the effectiveness of a straightforward architectural framework to mitigate the impact of jailbreak attacks on end users.

papers.summary: This paper examines the consequences of straightforward jailbreak vulnerabilities in conversational models. The researchers compare outputs across several systems and languages, using human annotations to inspect harmful recommendations, misinformation and biased responses. They also evaluate a defensive wrapper intended to prevent unsafe interactions. The important result for HMEG is not an attack recipe but the evidence that apparent safeguards can fail in ways that surface-word matching may miss. The work motivates semantic and instruction-aware analysis and careful downstream evaluation. HMEG remains an English-only prompt detector, so the paper’s cross-language tests and generated-response outcomes should not be described as capabilities or reproduced results of this website.

papers.title: Embedding-based classifiers can detect prompt injection attacks
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are seeing significant adoption in every type of organization due to their exceptional generative capabilities. However, LLMs are found to be vulnerable to various adversarial attacks, particularly prompt injection attacks, which trick them into producing harmful or inappropriate content. Adversaries execute such attacks by crafting malicious prompts to deceive the LLMs. In this paper, we propose a novel approach based on embedding-based Machine Learning (ML) classifiers to protect LLM-based applications against this severe threat. We leverage three commonly used embedding models to generate embeddings of malicious and benign prompts and utilize ML classifiers to predict whether an input prompt is malicious. Out of several traditional ML methods, we achieve the best performance with classifiers built using Random Forest and XGBoost. Our classifiers outperform state-of-the-art prompt injection classifiers available in open-source implementations, which use encoder-only neural networks.
papers.abstractPermission: Verbatim source abstract; line wraps and ligatures normalized. CC BY 4.0; attribution retained.
papers.summary: The researchers test whether malicious prompts can be recognized from embedding vectors using conventional machine learning. They deduplicate public sources into 467,057 prompts and use a stratified 80/20 split. OpenAI, GTE and MiniLM embeddings feed logistic regression, random forest and XGBoost classifiers. Random Forest with OpenAI embeddings gives the strongest reported results in their comparison, while the paper discusses precision–recall trade-offs against other detectors. The study primarily addresses direct injection and leaves other settings for future work. For HMEG, it supports investigating an embedding-plus-classifier Meaning Expert, but it does not establish the performance of HMEG’s selected encoder or hierarchical fusion.

papers.title: JailbreakTracer: Explainable Detection of Jailbreaking Prompts in LLMs Using Synthetic Data Generation
papers.abstract: The emergence of Large Language Models (LLMs) has revolutionized natural language processing (NLP), enabling remarkable advancements across various applications. However, these models remain susceptible to adversarial prompts, commonly referred to as jailbreaks, which exploit their vulnerabilities to bypass ethical and safety constraints. These prompts manipulate LLMs to produce harmful or forbidden outputs, posing serious ethical and security challenges. In this study, we propose JailbreakTracer, a novel framework leveraging synthetic data generation and Explainable AI (XAI) to detect and classify jailbreaking prompts. We first construct two comprehensive datasets: a Toxic Prompt Classification Dataset, combining real-world and synthetic jailbreak prompts, and a Forbidden Question Reasoning Dataset, categorizing forbidden queries into 13 distinct scenarios with clear reasoning labels. Synthetic toxic prompts are generated using a fine-tuned GPT model, achieving an attack success rate of 95.1%, effectively addressing the class imbalance. Using transformer-based architectures, we train classifiers that achieved 97.25% accuracy in detecting jailbreak prompts and 100% accuracy in categorizing forbidden questions. Our approach integrates XAI techniques, such as LIME, to ensure interpretability and transparency in the model’s predictions. Extensive evaluations demonstrate the efficacy of JailbreakTracer in detecting and reasoning about jailbreak prompts, providing a critical step toward enhancing the safety and accountability of LLMs. The dataset and code are available on GitHub: https://github.com/faiyazabdullah/JailbreakTracer

papers.summary: JailbreakTracer studies detection and explanation of jailbreak prompts using both collected and synthetic examples. It builds a binary toxic-prompt corpus and a separate forbidden-question dataset with 13 categories. Fine-tuned transformer classifiers, including BERT and RoBERTa, perform the classification, while LIME supplies token-level explanations. The abstract reports 97.25% accuracy for detection and 100% for categorization; these must remain separate tasks with their own experimental settings. The authors acknowledge controlled-data and synthetic-data limitations. HMEG can use this work to motivate transparent augmentation records and explanation checks, while independently measuring false positives and generalization on English prompts instead of transferring the paper’s performance claims.

papers.opportunity: Motivates clear augmentation provenance and explainability checks. HMEG must separately test false positives on unseen English data.
papers.findings: Abstract reports 97.25% jailbreak detection accuracy and 100% forbidden-question categorization accuracy. These are different tasks; they are not HMEG results.

papers.title: A Hybrid Perplexity-MAS Framework for Proactive Jailbreak Attack Detection in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Jailbreak attacks (JAs) represent a sophisticated subclass of adversarial threats wherein malicious actors craft strategically engineered prompts that subvert the intended operational boundaries of large language models (LLMs). These attacks exploit latent vulnerabilities in generative AI architectures, allowing adversaries to circumvent established safety protocols and illicitly induce the model to output prohibited, unethical, or harmful content. The emergence of such exploits underscores critical gaps in the security and controllability of modern AI systems, raising profound concerns about their societal impact and deployment in sensitive environments. In response, this study introduces an innovative defense framework that synergistically integrates language model perplexity analysis with a Multi-Agent System (MAS)-oriented detection architecture. This hybrid design aims to fortify the resilience of LLMs by proactively identifying and neutralizing jailbreak attempts, thereby ensuring the protection of user privacy and ethical integrity. The experimental setup adopts a query-driven adversarial probing strategy, in which jailbreak prompts are dynamically generated and injected into the open-source LLaMA-2 model to systematically explore potential vulnerabilities. To ensure rigorous validation, the proposed framework will be evaluated using a custom jailbreak detection benchmark encompassing metrics such as Attack Success Rate (ASR), Defense Success Rate (DSR), Defense Pass Rate (DPR), False Positive Rate, Benign Pass Rate (BPR), and End-to-End Latency. Through iterative experimentation and continuous refinement, this work endeavors to advance the defensive capabilities of LLM-based systems, enabling more trustworthy, secure, and ethically aligned deployment of generative AI in real-world environments.

papers.title: Detecting Language Model Attacks with Perplexity
papers.abstractPermission: Original abstract linked at the official source; republication permission has not been verified.
papers.summary: The authors study machine-generated adversarial suffixes using GPT-2 perplexity and prompt length. They show why a simple perplexity cutoff can reject legitimate prompts, especially very short inputs with unusual token sequences. A LightGBM classifier combines length and perplexity, with its decision threshold selected on validation data using F2. In the reported test, the classifier detects many generated suffix attacks but misses all 23 human-crafted jailbreak examples. This is evidence for a specialized structural signal, not a universal jailbreak detector. For HMEG, it motivates combining the Pattern Expert with semantic and instruction experts and explicitly testing short benign prompts.
papers.objective: Detect machine-generated adversarial suffix prompts while reducing false positives from perplexity-only rules.
papers.methodology: Compute GPT-2 perplexity and sequence length; train LightGBM; tune the threshold on a separate validation set for F2; evaluate a held-out test set.
datasets: Regular prompt datasets described in the source
papers.results: Table 1: 355 detected machine-generated attacks, 4 missed, and 23/23 human-crafted examples missed. Table 2: overall test F2 94.2%; F2 99.1% when human-crafted examples are excluded. These results cannot support a general jailbreak-detection claim.
papers.limitations: The authors note incomplete coverage of real interactions, dependence on one attack-generation setup and exclusive use of GPT-2 for perplexity. The method does not detect the studied human-crafted jailbreaks.
papers.opportunity: Combine structural evidence with other HMEG experts and audit short-prompt false positives separately.
papers.findings: Prompt length helps distinguish some short benign high-perplexity inputs from adversarial suffixes; structural signals alone miss human-crafted attacks.

papers.title: Prompt Injection Detection is Regime-Dependent: A Deployment-Aware Evaluation with Interpretable Structural Signals
papers.source: Prompt Injection Detection is Regime-Dependent_ A Deployment-Aware Evaluation with Interpretable Structural Signals - 2605.26999v1.pdf
papers.abstract: Prompt injection poses a critical threat to the safe deployment of large language models, yet existing detection approaches are typically evaluated under limited settings that do not reect real-world operating constraints. In this work, we present a deployment-aware evaluation of prompt injection detection using a multi-model and multi-regime experimental framework. We compare lexical, semantic, structural, and transformer-based detectors across multiple out-of-distribution settings, repeated data splits, and both ranking and thresholded deployment metrics. We introduce interpretable structural signals that capture hierarchy overrides, system prompt spoong, role redenition, and evasion patterns, and assess their contribution both within sparse models and in combination with strong encoder baselines. Our results show that detection performance is highly regime-dependent and sensitive to threshold selection, with no single model dominating across all settings. Transformerbased models achieve the strongest overall performance, while structural signals provide modest but consistent gains in certain regimes and improve low false positive rate behaviour in harder scenarios. These ndings highlight the gap between ranking performance and deployment eectiveness and underscore the importance of evaluating prompt injection defences under realistic operational constraints. Code will be released.
papers.abstractPermission: Verbatim source abstract; line wraps and ligatures normalized. CC BY 4.0; attribution retained.
papers.summary: This study compares prompt-injection detectors under several evaluation regimes rather than assuming that one test set represents deployment. Lexical, semantic, structural and transformer-based systems are tested with repeated splits and out-of-distribution sources. The authors introduce interpretable instruction-boundary signals and select thresholds using validation data only. They report that no model dominates every regime and that strong ranking scores can coexist with weak behavior at conservative false-positive rates. The paper gives HMEG a useful evaluation template: preserve source boundaries, examine benign hard negatives and measure low-FPR recall. It supports testing the proposed architecture, not claiming that hierarchical routing already solves distribution shift.
papers.objective: Evaluate how detector effectiveness changes across deployment regimes and operating thresholds.
papers.methodology: Compare lexical, semantic, structural and encoder families; choose thresholds only on validation predictions, freeze them, and test ID and multiple OOD regimes.
datasets: 6,424 total records across ID and OOD regimes (Table 4); ID train 694, validation 149, test 149
papers.results: Table 5 reports ID RoBERTa + IBVS Total macro-F1 0.9541 ± 0.0354. Strong ranking performance does not consistently imply strong low-FPR behavior across regimes.
papers.limitations: Short prompts offer limited evidence; benign security text can resemble attacks. Authors call for targeted slices and broader deployment testing.
papers.opportunity: Motivates separate English OOD evaluation, frozen threshold selection and false-positive analysis. Similar signals do not prove HMEG’s router is effective.
papers.findings: Table 5 reports ID RoBERTa + IBVS Total macro-F1 0.9541 ± 0.0354. Strong ranking performance does not consistently imply strong low-FPR behavior across regimes.
papers.calibration: Validation-only threshold selection; fixed on test and OOD

papers.title: RigorLLM: Resilient Guardrails for Large Language Models against Undesired Content
papers.venue: Proceedings of the 41st International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 235
papers.abstractPermission: Original abstract linked at the official source; republication permission has not been verified.
papers.summary: The authors study harmful-content detection when an attacker tries to evade a guardrail. RigorLLM combines synthetic training-data generation, a defensive suffix and a fusion mechanism using nearest-neighbor classification and language models. Its evaluation includes ToxicChat and adversarially modified inputs, with comparisons against moderation services and other guardrails. The authors report stronger harmful-content detection and resilience within their experiments. These findings concern a multi-component defense, not a small standalone text classifier. For HMEG, the relevant idea is combining complementary evidence while evaluating robustness separately from ordinary classification. HMEG instead investigates detection-mechanism experts and confidence-based routing; it does not implement RigorLLM.
papers.objective: Improve harmful-content detection and resilience to adversarial inputs.
papers.methodology: Generate synthetic data using an energy-based model and Langevin dynamics; construct a defensive suffix with minimax optimization; fuse nearest-neighbor and language-model decisions.
datasets: Adversarial evaluation inputs described in the paper
papers.results: The authors report stronger detection than evaluated baselines on their harmful-content and jailbreak settings. Consult the source tables for settings; these are not HMEG results.
papers.limitations: Not specified in the source.
papers.opportunity: Test whether heterogeneous expert fusion improves HMEG robustness without the runtime cost of a multi-LLM guardrail.
papers.findings: Data augmentation, defensive input transformation and prediction fusion are evaluated as complementary defenses.
papers.scopeNote: HMEG relevance is an interpretation, not an implementation of this paper. The current HMEG research evaluates English prompts only.
papers.ensemble: Fusion of KNN and LLM predictions

papers.title: SmoothLLM: Defending Large Language Models Against Jailbreaking Attacks
papers.abstractPermission: Original abstract linked at the official source; republication permission has not been verified.
papers.summary: SmoothLLM explores a defense based on the sensitivity of adversarial prompts to small character changes. It creates perturbed copies of a prompt, queries the protected language model and aggregates the resulting safety judgments. The authors evaluate several jailbreak attack families on AdvBench and also examine normal instruction-following performance. Their experiments show robustness improvements in the studied conditions, with a trade-off: stronger perturbations can damage legitimate task performance. This motivates HMEG testing for unusual formatting while monitoring benign false positives. HMEG does not rewrite prompts or repeatedly query an LLM; its Format Expert classifies character-level evidence as one input to the guardrail.
papers.objective: Mitigate jailbreaks through randomized prompt perturbation and aggregation.
papers.methodology: Create multiple character-perturbed copies, query the target LLM and aggregate outputs according to safety judgments.
models: Protected LLMs including Llama 2 and Vicuna
papers.results: The paper reports reduced attack success under the evaluated attacks. Figure 9 shows ordinary instruction-following degradation as perturbation strength increases; robustness should be read together with this utility trade-off.
papers.limitations: The authors identify the trade-off between perturbation strength and nominal task performance, and note that safety judges can mislabel responses to heavily perturbed prompts.
papers.opportunity: Measure HMEG robustness to character obfuscation without equating unusual formatting with malicious intent.
papers.findings: Randomized transformations can improve resistance while also harming legitimate task utility.
papers.scopeNote: HMEG relevance is an interpretation, not an implementation of this paper. The current HMEG research evaluates English prompts only.
papers.ensemble: Aggregate decisions from multiple perturbed prompt copies
steps: Select a compatible response or refusal

papers.title: SoK: Evaluating Jailbreak Guardrails for Large Language Models
papers.abstractPermission: Original abstract linked at the official source; republication permission has not been verified.
papers.summary: This systematization organizes jailbreak guardrails and evaluates their security, efficiency and utility together. The authors classify defenses by intervention stage, technical approach, safety granularity, response behavior, applicability and explainability. They then examine how protection, computational cost and rejection of benign requests interact. Their analysis includes false-positive behavior on OR-Bench and shows that method labels alone do not establish a universal efficiency or safety ranking. Hardware-specific measurements and incomplete coverage of evolving attacks limit generalization. For HMEG, this motivates reporting latency, false positives and held-out attack performance alongside detection scores, instead of presenting one accuracy number as complete evidence of quality.
papers.objective: Systematize guardrail mechanisms and evaluate their security-efficiency-utility trade-offs.
papers.methodology: Six-dimensional taxonomy plus empirical assessment of guardrail security, latency/memory and benign-request utility.
datasets: Multiple jailbreak attack evaluations described in the source
papers.results: The evaluation finds substantial variation in protection, resource costs and false positives across mechanisms. Figure 2 and the cross-attack analysis should be read with their specific settings; no universal ranking is inferred.
papers.limitations: The authors note hardware-specific efficiency measurements on NVIDIA H800 GPUs and limits to exhaustive coverage of guardrail methods and evolving attacks.
papers.opportunity: Measure HMEG false positives, routing cost and generalization within one controlled protocol.
papers.findings: Guardrail comparisons require security, efficiency and benign-user utility to be assessed together.
papers.scopeNote: HMEG relevance is an interpretation, not an implementation of this paper. The current HMEG research evaluates English prompts only.

papers.title: WildGuard: Open One-stop Moderation Tools for Safety Risks, Jailbreaks, and Refusals of LLMs
papers.venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 37, Datasets and Benchmarks Track
papers.abstractPermission: Original abstract linked at the official source; republication permission has not been verified.
papers.summary: WildGuard addresses three related moderation tasks: identifying harmful user intent, judging harmful model responses and recognizing refusals. The authors construct WildGuardMix with 92,000 labeled examples and instruction-tune Mistral-7b-v0.3 for a unified output format. Evaluation covers WildGuardTest and multiple public safety benchmarks. The paper reports improvements across the three tasks, but notes that synthetic data, finite model coverage and differences in harm taxonomies can limit transfer. For HMEG, the useful lessons concern separating input risk from output harm, auditing synthetic-data coverage and measuring false refusals. HMEG remains an English input detector and does not implement WildGuard or its complete moderation workflow.
papers.objective: Build an open moderation system covering prompt harmfulness, response harmfulness and refusal detection.
papers.methodology: Construct a balanced multitask moderation dataset and instruction-tune Mistral-7b-v0.3 to produce three task-specific outputs.
features: User prompt and optional model response
datasets: WildGuardMix: 92K labeled examples across 13 risk categories
papers.results: Table 3 reports WildGuard mean F1 86.1% for prompt harmfulness across five public benchmarks and 82.4% for response harmfulness across four public benchmarks. The tasks and datasets differ from HMEG evaluation.
papers.limitations: The authors note heavy reliance on synthetic inputs, limited coverage of real user and model-response distributions, and differences between harm taxonomies.
papers.opportunity: Keep HMEG jailbreak labels distinct from harmful-topic and refusal labels, and audit coverage of benign prompts.
papers.findings: A unified safety model can address input harm, response harm and refusal detection, with task-specific evaluation.
papers.scopeNote: HMEG relevance is an interpretation, not an implementation of this paper. The current HMEG research evaluates English prompts only.
